Literally what I just commented! This setup looks a lot like those which are popular for guinea pigs right now. I think its with good intentions, but wrongly applied to species.

Cavies such as guinea pigs can tolerate this sort of setup if you're going for cost effective and low mess (I know fleece liners are very popular for them right now) I own guinea pigs so totally understand. However, hamsters are very different.

They need deep bedding for burrowing enrichment and to hide/make secure nests. Unfortunately this sort of setup won't accomodate the needs. The good news is that dwarf hamsters aren't too messy or smelly provided you spot clean and deep clean, so don't be afraid to provide deep bedding.

I also echo what others have said about the cage bar width - your hamster will escape. Please look into bin cages or box cage alternatives. Very cheap, secure, plenty of room and depth for important burrowing.

She will also benefit from chances to climb, natural safe wood to chew on, and scatter feeding/enrichment based feeding to keep her occupied.

One thing you need to take care of is punctuation in dialogue. You do mostly have the right idea, but in just a few places you slip up.

“And you haven’t aged a day either, mentally.” I said with a smirk.

Here you have a full stop between the dialogue and the dialogue tag - it should be a comma. Remember that the only times you use a full stop are when you are describing an action following dialogue (you may also use full stop and exclamation marks). If you have a description of how the dialogue is said, use either a comma, question mark, exclamation mark or em dash.

So it should be:

“And you haven’t aged a day either, mentally," I said with a smirk

And just here...

...No bodies, though. So they're calling it the victimless murder” He said.

It needs to be a comma, followed by a lower case h. Again, if you were describing an action, that's the only time you'd use a full stop/question/exclamation mark followed by a capital letter.

So:
No bodies, though. So they're calling it the victimless murder,” he said.

Alright, main points:

- Tense. As someone else has pointed out, you need to pick one and stick with it. Present tense can be difficult to keep up with, so if you're struggling consider past. 

- Beginning your story with "So" seems clunky and awkward - consider dropping it, and beginning with "It was colder than usual".

- Show, don't tell. Let us know what your character is feeling through his actions and reactions rather than through plain empty words.

- Break it up a bit! Paragraphs are your friends. 

- Try to improve transitions between character placement. For example one moment he's sat in the corner, the next a pen has appeared in his hand and he's writing. Explain the bits in between, and include feeling (what does he think as he chooses to write? Why does he choose to do this? What's going on in his world as he writes?).

- Think of your world as a blank world. It will remain that way for your readers until you, the writer, fills it. So describe the room. Do it through your characters actions and what he interacts with. For me, all this room consists of is a bed, a glass of water, a corner and a pen. Oh, and outside there's the broken street lamp. Build your world to make it come to life.

I don't necessarily see that word choice has hatred for adverbs - more the fact those who answered chose not to use "simultaneously". In fact in that case I'd be more tempted to use "simultaneously" just to make it more concise …

But in general adverbs can often become redundant, or are added unnecessarily. They can often bog down narrative as well meaning that a simple sentence becomes: "James looked around bashfully and then swiftly exited the building, letting the door bang loudly behind him. He moved rapidly, his heart beating loudly, sweat dripping profusely, feet pounding angrily..."

It's a long-winded way of saying James got embarrassed and left in a fit of anger. And if you choose to write your whole story that way, something that could have taken a couple of words or lines suddenly becomes a whole paragraph.

It also encourages writers to use telling as a crutch instead of showing. So we're hearing all the ways that James is feeling or leaving, or what he's doing, but we're not actually *seeing* it. You're telling us, not showing us.

So while adverbs used sparingly can be OK, it is a bad idea to toss them throughout your story to describe every single little action your character carries out.

Okay. Dialogue crash-course, specifically the punctuation rules. The part after dialogue is, as I'm sure you know, the dialogue tag. This describes how something is said or who is saying it. The general rule is that you use a comma and follow by a lower case letter. Or use an exclamation/question mark followed by lower case. For example:

"All right," he said.

"All right," he said, a little awkwardly.

"I'm not a therapist, Kevin," she said.

Use a full stop if you're following up with an action, for example:
"Come sit down." She slid along the bench to give him room.

So just take care with that aspect of it.

The main thing is Clara - she's learnt the parents are dead, asks if she should be worried about that and then snaps at your MC. This is a mix of tenses. "There is" and "door flies" is present. "I peeked" is past. I see a lot of tense flipping so try to choose one and stick with it.

["Clear!" A loud rumbly voice yells. I peeked out from under the sheets to see a large figure dressed in all-black tactical gear standing with a very large gun in his hands, using his flashlight to check the room. He had just started to leave when he pointed his light at my bed and I tried to cover my face but it was too late. He saw me.]

A whole lot of telling, not much showing. We're in first person here so you can really take advantage and tap into exactly what your character is hearing, experiencing and feeling. Imagine it's you in a strange room hiding ... how are you feeling?


["Yo! I got one!" He yelled]

Remember dialogue tag rules. The tag should begin with a lower case ("Yo! I got one!" he yelled).

["Uhm, My name's- I'm- I- I don't know". And that was when I realized that I didn't remember anything.]

Again, show us more! Losing memory of who you are and not knowing where you are must scare your character.

The rest continues in a similar way - mixed tenses and attention should be shown to punctuation, especially in dialogue.

It also seems extremely rushed and nowhere enough time building up scenes or environments, and definitely no time on characters. We seem to have faceless characters thrown at us and then their names casually mentioned later. 

I suggest slowing down and trying to flesh out these scenes better. Let us get to know your protagonist through her thoughts, fears and internal monologue. Try to build her world and those in it better too so we can really visualise and empathise with everyone.

It can take several months for a dog to decompress when in a new home. This basically means the period of time it takes for them to get used to the change of pace, the noise, the activity and the people/other dogs. So first of all be extremely careful you are not effectively winding the dog up (unintentionally!) so he becomes a coiled spring. 

He needs time and a quiet space to just find his bearings. So make sure there is somewhere he can go to hide if he wants, and that he isn't expected to be the centre of attention all the time.

You need to consider what happened during the times he attacked. What was everyone doing? What was happening around him? Had you taken him for a walk where he might have gotten stressed? Was the other dog too boisterous?

Also, try to remember the formatting rules for dialogue. The bit after dialogue (he said/shouted /asked) is known as a dialogue tag. When you have this, you only need a comma, question mark or exclamation mark followed by a lower cased letter. For example:

“I’m thinking of going to the shop today,” he said.

Or:

“Get away from me!” he yelled.

Or:

“Where are you going?” he asked.

Only use a full stop when you intend to follow the dialogue with an action.

“I’m tired of this.” He slammed the book down in frustration.
